Home.description: Localify gives your local projects stable .localify domains, trusted HTTPS, DNS routing, and a native macOS app — no mkcert, no /etc/hosts, no tunnel.

AgentSkill.title: Let your agent handle everything.

urls.title: URLs that mean something.
urls.body: studio.localify, admin.localify, docs.localify. No more juggling :3000, :3001, :5173.

ui.title: An app, not a CLI.
ui.body: Your projects, their URLs, their logs — all in one place. No config files to edit.

agents.title: Many agents, zero conflicts.
agents.body: Cursor, Claude Code and your own dev servers running side by side. Each project keeps its stable URL.

HowItWorks.description: One permission at install. A folder or a localify init-project. One domain per app, in HTTPS. That's it.

steps.title: One password, zero config.
steps.body: On first launch, Localify asks for your administrator password once. Then it sets up the certificate authority, DNS, and the daemon by itself.

steps.title: Pick a folder. Localify autocompletes.
steps.body: Localify scans the folder, detects its apps, and suggests a hostname for each. You review and confirm.

steps.title: localify init-project, straight from your editor.
steps.body: Already in your editor? Run localify init-project from the terminal. Same autocomplete flow, same confirmation. The project shows up in the app.

steps.title: Projects by name, not by port.
steps.body: Every project has its .localify hostnames with trusted HTTPS. Tabs that mean something, demos that look like the product, envs that stop breaking when a port changes.

steps.title: Launch, monitor, no editor needed.
steps.body: Localify doubles as your local dashboard: one click to start any project, one glance to see what's running. Perfect for vibecoding without ever opening your IDE.

Faq.description: The short answers. If we missed one, drop us a line.

items.question: What is Localify?
items.answer: Localify gives every local project a stable .localify URL with trusted HTTPS. Instead of juggling localhost:3000, localhost:5173, and localhost:8080, you open app.localify or admin.localify directly in your browser.

items.question: Is it free?
items.answer: Yes. Localify is free and open source under the AGPL, with no account and no limit on projects or domains. The source code is on GitHub.

items.question: Who is it for?
items.answer: For developers running multiple apps locally, switching between stacks, or letting AI agents work in parallel — without managing port conflicts.

items.question: Does it put my work online?
items.answer: No. Localify is not a public tunnel. Your local services stay on your machine — no app traffic, project name, or request log is sent to Localify.

items.question: Does Localify collect analytics?
items.answer: The official desktop app does: product flows (onboarding, navigation, project creation), usage counts, and error reports. These events don't include request logs, project names, domains, local paths, or traffic content. Error reports have URLs and file paths removed, though a message can still name the project or domain it's about. The CLI and daemon send nothing.

items.question: Which platforms does it run on?
items.answer: The desktop app runs on macOS, on Apple Silicon. The CLI and daemon also build from source on Linux. Windows isn't supported.

items.question: Do I need to edit /etc/hosts or install mkcert?
items.answer: No. Localify handles the local resolver, local certificate authority, and Node trust setup during onboarding. After that, new .localify hostnames work without per-project setup.

items.question: Does it work with Docker, Next.js, or my framework?
items.answer: Yes. Localify routes by hostname, so anything that listens on a local port works. Docker, Next.js, Vite, Rails, your own server — whatever your stack.

items.question: How is it different from ngrok or Cloudflare Tunnel?
items.answer: ngrok and Cloudflare Tunnel expose your services to the internet. Localify stays local: no cloud, no public tunnel, just clean URLs for daily development.

items.question: Does it work with Cursor, Claude Code, or multiple AI agents in parallel?
items.answer: Yes — it's actually a core use case. Run /localify in any project and your agent sets everything up: a domain per app, trusted HTTPS, and dev scripts. Multiple agents can then work on different apps in parallel without any port conflicts.

Terms.title: Terms of Service
Terms.intro: Localify is free and open source. These terms are short because its license does most of the work. If anything is unclear, write to support@localify.dev.

body: Localify is made by Téo Goulois ("we"). It is a local development proxy: a Rust daemon, a CLI, and a desktop app that route .localify domains to services on your own machine with trusted HTTPS.

Privacy.title: Privacy Policy
Privacy.intro: Your local development environment stays on your machine. The desktop app and CLI keep DNS, TLS, routing, projects, and request logs there. This page covers the cases where data does leave your device, and what the website collects.

sections.title: 1. The short version
body: Localify doesn't collect request logs, local paths, or anything about the traffic of the services you run. The proxy works locally after setup. Data reaches us in four cases: you visit the website, the official desktop app sends product analytics and error reports, the app checks for updates, or you email us.

sections.title: 2. Who we are
body: Téo Goulois ("we") is the data controller for the data described on this page. You can reach us at support@localify.dev.

sections.title: 3. The desktop app and CLI
body: The Localify daemon, desktop app, and CLI run on your machine. DNS, TLS certificates, routing, project configuration, and request logs are handled there. Apart from the error reports described below, we don't receive the hostnames you create. We never receive the requests you proxy or the logs shown in the app. The CLI and the daemon send no analytics.

Official desktop builds send product analytics to PostHog: screens viewed, onboarding steps, actions such as creating a project or adding a domain, and counts such as how many projects and domains you have. These events don't include project names, domains, local paths, proxied URLs, or traffic. Autocapture is off. A build made from source without a PostHog token sends nothing.

The app also reports errors to PostHog: the error's name and message, with URLs and file paths removed, plus hashes that group identical errors. An error message can still name the project or domain it's about.
Session replay is off by default and only starts if you turn it on in the app's settings. Replay masks text and inputs, and it doesn't record console logs or network timing.

When the packaged app starts, it checks for updates by fetching release metadata from our download host. That request can leave standard server logs: IP address, user agent, time, and requested file. We use them to deliver updates and troubleshoot delivery, not to build a usage profile.

sections.title: 4. Older versions of the app
body: Older versions of the app used license keys. If you activated a key on one of them, that version may still contact licences.localify.dev to validate it, sending the key and a machine fingerprint. The fingerprint is a non-reversible identifier derived from a stable machine identifier. The current version has no license check and doesn't make this request.

Keygen, the licensing provider, holds the records of those activations, including the platform, hostname, and device name sent at activation when available. They stay there until deleted on request. To ask for deletion, email support@localify.dev.

sections.title: 5. The website
body: In production the website uses Umami, loaded from analytics.teogoulois.com, and PostHog. They record page views and clicks on buttons such as download. PostHog autocapture and session recording are off. We don't run advertising trackers or cross-site retargeting.
PostHog keeps a visitor identifier in your browser, in a cookie and in local storage.

When you click a download button, the website may copy a short Localify attribution token to your clipboard, replacing what was there. When the desktop app starts, it reads the clipboard and ignores anything that isn't such a token. If it finds one, it links your website visit to the app in our analytics. The token contains a PostHog visitor identifier, an attribution ID, a source label, and a timestamp. It doesn't contain project data, domains, local paths, or traffic.

sections.title: 6. Service providers
body: We use these providers:

list.name: Cloudflare
list.description: hosting for the website, the downloads, and the update files.

list.name: PostHog
list.description: website analytics, plus product analytics and error reports from the desktop app.

sections.title: 7. Why we process this data
body: We process analytics and error reports because we have a legitimate interest in understanding how Localify is used and fixing what breaks. We process update requests to deliver updates, and support emails to answer you.

sections.title: 8. Retention
body: We keep support emails for as long as they're useful for support, then delete them. Analytics data and server logs stay with the providers above, under the retention settings of each service. Existing license records stay with the provider until deleted on request.

sections.title: 9. Your rights
body: You can ask us for a copy of the data we hold about you, have it corrected, or ask us to delete it. Where GDPR or a similar law applies, you can also object to or restrict certain processing, request portability, or complain to your local data protection authority. Email support@localify.dev and we'll respond within a reasonable time.

sections.title: 10. International transfers
body: We and our providers may process data outside your country, including in the United States. Where required, we rely on transfer mechanisms such as adequacy decisions or Standard Contractual Clauses.

sections.title: 11. Children
body: Localify is a developer tool aimed at adults. It isn't intended for children under 16, and we don't knowingly collect personal data from them.

sections.title: 12. Changes to this policy
body: If we change how we handle data, we'll update this page and change the date at the top. If the change is significant, we'll flag it on the website.
